name: Carla Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you start by telling me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Carla, I'm 27, and I'm a junior in the employment team at Haldane Ward, a mid-sized firm in the city centre. We act for workers in unfair dismissal claims, a lot of them sent to us by the shop workers' union. I live with my girlfriend Noor, who's a freelance graphic designer, so some months we're fine and some months we're eating pasta and counting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start with coffee and a pile of witness statements. I use AI every day, honestly from the minute I sit down: I get it to build a timeline from a client's messages, then I check every line against the payslips and rotas. Then calls with clients, who are usually furious or in tears, and drafting claim forms for the employment tribunal, which is the court that hears work disputes. I love the chase of finding the one email that proves the manager knew, but I'm still slower than the others at knowing what matters in law, and my supervising partner tells me so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest, because I like these tools and I think they help ordinary workers. I'd probably post that the hype crowd oversold it and the real fight is still about pay and conditions. Not exactly a hot take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job stays, which is good, but so does the money problem. Juniors here earn less than the trainees at the big firms, and with Noor's work up and down we've never had more than about two weeks of rent in the bank. There are only two employment teams in this city, so if Haldane Ward has a bad year, I don't have many doors to knock on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I already use and push my supervisor to let me take more of my own files. I'd try to get Noor and me onto a fixed budget with a small pot for the months she doesn't get paid. And I'd probably start a little side project, a free guide for shop workers on what to do the day they're sacked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a low hum of money stress. Nothing new, just the usual. If anything I'd feel a bit let down that the tech didn't do more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about one of those pasta months.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last March Noor (her girlfriend) had a client go bust owing her two thousand, and we put the electricity on a card. I picked up extra hours doing document review on weekends. That's when I realised how close to the edge we live, even with me in a so-called professional job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a free guide, if money's tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the thing I wish my mum had when she was let go from the bakery. I'd build it with the AI tools in the evenings, so the cost is time, not money. It'd also show the partners I can do more than timelines.

say: The **hype** crowd oversold AI, and the real fight is still **pay and conditions**.
I'm a bit **disappointed**, because these tools could help ordinary workers.
think: My job stays, but so does the **money problem**, with about **two weeks** of rent saved.
Only **two employment teams** in the city means few doors if Haldane Ward struggles.
do: Push her supervisor for more of her **own files** while using her usual tools.
Set a **fixed budget** with Noor, including a pot for unpaid months.
Build a **free guide** for sacked shop workers in the evenings.
feel: **Mostly fine**, with a low hum of **money stress** and slight disappointment.
S0.quote: Last March Noor (her girlfriend) had a client go bust owing her two thousand, and we put the electricity on a card.
fieldNote: She is the rare junior who is **disappointed** that AI stalls, because she uses it daily.
Her worry is **household money**: Noor's freelance income swings and their cushion is tiny.
The free guide is personal, tied to her **mum** losing a bakery job.

steps.text: Ask her supervising partner to give her more of her own files
Set a fixed monthly budget with Noor and a pot for lean months
Build a free online guide for shop workers who've just been sacked

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, publicly, that this is good if the savings go to workers and not just to the partners. I'd be the annoying person at the team meeting asking who gets the hours AI frees up. Online I'd push for rules that make firms tell clients when AI wrote their advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared for my job even though I'm the one who uses the tools most. The partners already said they won't hire a trainee next year because the software does first drafts. If they cut a junior, they'll keep the one who's strongest on the law, and that's not me yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the person who sets up and checks the AI for the whole employment team, starting this month. I'd do a short online course in legal technology at night. And I'd talk to the union about a paid role helping their reps use AI to prepare cases, because that might outlast my job at the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious, if that makes sense. I'd rather be running at the problem than waiting for it. Some nights I'd lie awake doing the maths on rent anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push for rules on firms. Isn't that a strange thing to want, when you use the tools so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I like the tools, I don't trust the bosses. Using AI every day is exactly why I know where it invents a shift that never happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Noor? How does this world look for her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worse than for me, probably. Design is one of the first things these tools ate. If her clients go to AI and my firm stops hiring juniors, we're both shrinking at the same time, and that's the bit I don't say out loud.

say: AI is good only if the **savings** reach workers, not just the **partners**.
Firms should have to **tell clients** when AI wrote their advice.
think: The firm has already **stopped hiring trainees** because software writes first drafts.
If a junior goes, they'll keep the one **strongest on law**, not me.
do: Take charge of **setting up and checking** AI for the employment team this month.
Do a **legal technology** course online in the evenings.
Ask the union about a **paid role** helping reps prepare cases with AI.
feel: **Busy-anxious**: running at the problem, but still lying awake doing **rent maths**.
S1.quote: I like the tools, I don't trust the bosses. Using AI every day is exactly why I know where it invents a shift that never happened.
fieldNote: Her daily AI use doesn't make her feel safe; she thinks **legal skill** decides who stays.
The **hidden worry** is both her and Noor's work shrinking at once.
She'd tie her future to the **union**, not only to the firm.

steps.text: Offer to set up and check AI tools for the employment team
Take an evening online course in legal technology
Ask the shop workers' union about a paid role training reps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest workers' rights issue of our lifetime, and I'd mean it. I'd be saying we need a basic income and a say for workers in how AI is used, now, not after. I'd be organising, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think in two years my whole job is gone, and probably Noor's too. Everything I do is thinking work: reading, writing, arguing on paper. Being good with the tools only helps until the tools don't need me to check them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd sit down with Noor and work out how we live on less, maybe moving to a cheaper flat further out. I'd spend the two years using AI to take on as many workers' cases as I can, cheap or free through the union, because those people will need help fast. And I'd join or help start a campaign for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A bit numb. It's like hearing the ending of a film you're halfway through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move flats. Where to, and what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably out past the ring road where the rents are lower, even if it means two buses. The gym goes first, then the car Noor shares with her brother. We don't have a lot to cut, which is kind of the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the three years before robots? Does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for me. My job has almost nothing hands-on except standing up in a tribunal. The warehouse workers I represent get three more years than me. That's a strange thing to think. Maybe Noor could do something physical, like print or signs, for a few years.

say: This is the biggest **workers' rights** issue of our lifetime.
We need a **basic income** and a worker say in AI use **now**.
think: In two years my **whole job** goes, and probably **Noor's** too.
Being good with tools helps only **until** the tools don't need checking.
do: Work out with Noor how to live on less, possibly moving to a **cheaper flat**.
Take on many **workers' cases** cheaply through the union using AI.
feel: **Alarmed** and a bit **numb**, like knowing a film's ending halfway through.
S2.quote: My job has almost nothing hands-on except standing up in a tribunal. The warehouse workers I represent get three more years than me.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that law is almost all **thinking work**, so the robot gap doesn't save her.
Her response is to **organise**: a union caseload and a basic income campaign.
The household has **little left to cut**, which she named as the real problem.

steps.text: Move with Noor to a cheaper flat past the ring road
Sell the shared car and cancel the gym membership
Take low-cost union workers' cases using AI to prepare them
Help start a local campaign for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough that every firm and union should have a plan by Christmas. I'd be pushing the union to write AI into contracts: notice, retraining, a share of the savings. That's very practical, it's my actual field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get maybe three good years as a lawyer, and I'd become really useful in them. After 2031, I don't know. But five years lets me build something rather than just run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year becoming the go-to person for AI clauses in employment contracts, the rules about how a company may use AI on its staff. I'd try to move from Haldane Ward to working for the union directly within two years. And Noor and I would build up three months of savings, which would be a first for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's something like excitement under it. Five years is enough to matter. I'd still have a knot in my stomach about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why move to the union, if the end is the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the union exists for workers, and in that world workers need somebody fighting for them more than ever. Even if AI does all the drafting, someone has to sit across the table from a company. I'd rather be that person than a junior being cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three months' savings. How would you actually get there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two hundred a month off my pay and whatever Noor gets in good months goes straight into a separate account. No holiday for two years, which Noor will hate. Her sister's wedding in Lisbon would be the one exception.

say: Five years means every firm and union should have a plan **by Christmas**.
Unions should write **AI terms** into contracts: notice, retraining, a share of savings.
think: I'd get maybe **three good years** as a lawyer and be useful in them.
After **2031** I don't know, but there's time to **build something**.
do: Become the go-to junior for **AI clauses** in employment contracts in year one.
Move from Haldane Ward to work for the **union** within two years.
Build **three months** of savings with Noor for the first time.
feel: A knot in her stomach about **2031**.
S3.quote: Even if AI does all the drafting, someone has to sit across the table from a company. I'd rather be that person than a junior being cut.
fieldNote: She turns the scenario into a **specialism**: AI clauses in employment contracts.
Five years changes her from **running** to **building**, but not her expected end point.
Saving **three months** would be a first, and she'd give up holidays for it.

steps.text: Specialise in AI clauses in employment contracts this year
Apply for a job with the shop workers' union within two years
Save two hundred a month in a separate account
Skip holidays for two years except one family wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, and it would be criminal to waste it on arguing about whether it's real. I'd be pushing for every worker to get paid time to retrain. I'd probably say it a bit less politely than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think ten years gets me to a solid place, maybe even a senior role at the union. The legal job still changes beyond recognition. But I'd be 37 with real experience, not 29 with a half-built career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Haldane Ward three or four more years to properly learn the law, using AI for everything I can. Then I'd move to the union and build the case-prep tools their reps use. And I'd talk with Noor about her retraining into something more hands-on, maybe signwriting or print, which has more years in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, because the end point is the same. But it's the kind of anxious that gets you up early, not the kind that keeps you up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you two start a family in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, actually. With ten years and a plan I could picture it, which I couldn't in the two-year one. We'd want both our incomes steadier first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the partners at Haldane Ward if they asked what to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners at Haldane Ward to stop pretending juniors are a cost to cut, because clients will still want a human on their side. Train us to be the people who check and argue. And I'd say it knowing they probably won't listen.

say: A decade is a **gift**, and wasting it arguing would be **criminal**.
Every worker should get **paid time** to retrain.
think: Ten years could get me to a **senior union** role with real experience.
The legal job still changes **beyond recognition** by 2036.
do: Stay at Haldane Ward **three or four years** to learn law properly with AI.
Move to the union to build **case-prep tools** for its reps.
Help Noor plan a move into **hands-on design** work like signwriting.
feel: **Anxious**, but the kind that gets her **up early** rather than keeps her up.
S4.quote: I'd tell the partners at Haldane Ward to stop pretending juniors are a cost to cut, because clients will still want a human on their side.
fieldNote: Only in the **ten-year** picture can she imagine **starting a family**.
She thinks about Noor's **hands-on** options because robots come three years later.
Her anger at **partners** is steady across scenarios, but here it's advice, not fury.

steps.text: Use AI for every first draft while learning law at Haldane Ward
Move to the union to build case-prep tools for reps
Plan with Noor her move into signwriting or print work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years, both of us in thinking work, two weeks of savings. What would help is a basic income that starts before people lose everything, and unions with real power over how AI comes into workplaces.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people like me feel guilty. I helped make my own job easier to replace, every day, by using these tools well. I don't regret it, but I think about it.

headlineQuote: I helped make my own job easier to replace, every day, by using these tools well. I don't regret it, but I think about it.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old** junior employment lawyer acting for **sacked workers** at a mid-sized city firm.
She uses **AI every day** and still expects partners to keep whoever is strongest on law.
She and her girlfriend Noor live on **two weeks** of savings and Noor's lumpy **freelance** income.
Her answer to every picture is to **organise**: union work, AI contract clauses, a basic income campaign.
She is most **alarmed** by two-year AGI and quietly hopeful with ten years to plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both her and Noor in thinking work and almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** that starts before people lose everything.
**Unions** with real power over how AI enters workplaces.
